questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following organelles is bounded by a double membrane and possesses its own circular DNA?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) are semi-autonomous organelles with a double membrane and their own circular DNA, supporting the endosymbiotic theory.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The site within a eukaryotic cell where lipids are synthesised is the
questions.explanation: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and specialises in lipid synthesis and detoxification, unlike the rough ER which is studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A student examining a cell under the microscope observes a large central vacuole, a rigid wall, and plastids. This cell is most likely from
questions.explanation: A large central vacuole, cellulose cell wall, and plastids such as chloroplasts are diagnostic features of mature plant cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells?
options: Prokaryotic cells are always larger than eukaryotic cells
Only prokaryotic cells possess a cell membrane
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus while eukaryotic cells possess one
questions.explanation: The defining distinction is the presence of a true, membrane-bound nucleus in eukaryotes; prokaryotes have their genetic material free in the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: When a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplast away from the cell wall as water leaves a plant cell placed in a hypertonic (concentrated) solution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The process by which molecules move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration without the use of metabolic energy is
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive movement of molecules down a concentration gradient and requires no expenditure of cellular ATP.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Active transport differs from facilitated diffusion mainly because active transport
options: requires ATP and can move substances against their concentration gradient
always moves substances down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Active transport uses metabolic energy (ATP) to pump substances against their concentration gradient, unlike facilitated diffusion which is passive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of these is NOT a function of the Golgi apparatus?
options: Modification of proteins received from the rough ER
Synthesis of ATP through oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explanation: ATP synthesis via oxidative phosphorylation occurs in mitochondria, not the Golgi apparatus, which mainly processes, packages, and sorts proteins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The cell theory states that all of the following EXCEPT
options: all living organisms are composed of one or more cells
new cells arise from pre-existing cells
the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things
cells arise spontaneously from non-living matter
questions.explanation: Modern cell theory explicitly rejects spontaneous generation; it holds that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which classification kingdom contains eukaryotic, mostly unicellular organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium?
questions.explanation: Kingdom Protista comprises simple eukaryotic organisms, mostly unicellular, including protozoans like Amoeba and Paramecium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A virus is generally considered non-living outside a host cell mainly because it
options: is always larger than bacterial cells
has no genetic material at all
cannot reproduce independently without a host cell's machinery
questions.explanation: Viruses lack the cellular machinery for independent metabolism and replication, relying entirely on a host cell to reproduce, which places their 'living' status in question.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane is described as a fluid mosaic model mainly because
options: only carbohydrates are present in the membrane
the membrane consists of a single uniform layer of protein
phospholipids and proteins can move laterally within the membrane
the membrane is rigid and immovable
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a dynamic structure where phospholipids and embedded proteins can drift laterally within the bilayer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which structure regulates the entry of substances into the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Nuclear pores are channels in the nuclear envelope that regulate the passage of molecules such as RNA and proteins between the nucleus and cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why enzymes are described as biological catalysts?
options: They are consumed in every reaction they catalyse
They only work outside living cells
They speed up biochemical reactions without being permanently consumed
They increase the amount of product formed beyond the theoretical yield
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions and are regenerated at the end, so they are not permanently used up, defining them as catalysts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: An increase in temperature beyond an enzyme's optimum usually causes a sharp decline in reaction rate because
options: the enzyme's tertiary structure is disrupted, denaturing its active site
questions.explanation: Excess heat breaks the hydrogen and other bonds maintaining an enzyme's three-dimensional shape, denaturing the active site so it can no longer bind substrate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which taxonomic hierarchy, from broadest to most specific, is correctly arranged?
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: The standard Linnaean hierarchy runs from the broadest group, Kingdom, down to the most specific, Species, in the order given.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of these is a distinguishing feature of Kingdom Fungi?
options: Cell walls made of chitin and heterotrophic nutrition by absorption
Locomotion by cilia in all members
questions.explanation: Fungi have chitinous cell walls and feed heterotrophically by secreting enzymes externally and absorbing the digested nutrients.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The lysosome's principal role in a cell is to
options: digest worn-out organelles and foreign material using hydrolytic enzymes
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes that break down damaged organelles, food particles, and foreign invaders.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and air occurs across the walls of the
questions.explanation: Alveoli are thin-walled, richly capillary-supplied air sacs providing the large surface area needed for efficient gaseous exchange in the lungs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The chamber of the human heart that pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta is the
questions.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall and pumps oxygenated blood at high pressure into the aorta for distribution around the body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which blood vessels carry blood towards the heart?
questions.explanation: By definition, veins return blood to the heart, while arteries carry blood away from the heart, regardless of oxygen content.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, aids digestion mainly by
options: emulsifying fats to increase the surface area for lipase action
neutralising excess acid in the stomach
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area available for lipase to hydrolyse triglycerides efficiently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The end product of protein digestion that is absorbed into the bloodstream is
questions.explanation: Proteins are progressively broken down by proteases into peptides and finally amino acids, which are absorbed across the intestinal wall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which structure in the mammalian kidney is primarily responsible for the ultrafiltration of blood?
questions.explanation: The glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries within the Bowman's capsule, filters blood under pressure, forcing water and small solutes into the nephron.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Reabsorption of most glucose from the filtrate in the nephron occurs mainly in the
questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered glucose, amino acids, and ions back into the blood by active transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which hormone, secreted by the pancreas, lowers blood glucose level by promoting its uptake and storage as glycogen?
questions.explanation: Insulin stimulates cells, especially liver and muscle, to take up glucose from the blood and store it as glycogen, thereby lowering blood glucose.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The exchange of gases in a leaf occurs mainly through pores called
questions.explanation: Stomata, guarded by pairs of guard cells, are the main pores on leaf surfaces through which carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapour are exchanged.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which tissue in a vascular plant is responsible for the upward conduction of water and dissolved mineral salts?
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels and tracheids form continuous, non-living conducting tubes that transport water and minerals from roots to the rest of the plant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Translocation of manufactured food, mainly sucrose, from leaves to other parts of a plant occurs through the
questions.explanation: Phloem tissue, especially the sieve tubes and companion cells, transports organic solutes such as sucrose from source tissues to sink tissues.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The opening and closing of stomata is regulated mainly by changes in the
options: number of chloroplasts in epidermal cells
questions.explanation: Guard cells swell (turgid) to open stomata and become flaccid to close them, driven by osmotic movement of water linked to potassium ion concentration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of haemoglobin in respiration?
options: It binds reversibly with oxygen for transport around the body
It regulates the heart's rate of contraction
It digests carbohydrates in the small intestine
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it in respiring tissues, enabling oxygen transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In aerobic respiration, the greatest yield of ATP is generated during
options: oxidative phosphorylation in the electron transport chain
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain and chemiosmosis in the mitochondrial inner membrane generate the majority of ATP produced during aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces which two main end products?
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments glucose anaerobically into ethanol and carbon dioxide, a process exploited in brewing and baking.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which part of the human brain primarily controls balance and coordination of voluntary muscle movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum integrates sensory input to fine-tune motor commands, maintaining balance, posture, and coordinated movement.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A reflex action, such as withdrawing a hand from a hot object, is best described as
options: a response restricted only to plants
an action that always requires learning
a slow, deliberate response planned by the cerebrum
a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus not requiring conscious thought
questions.explanation: Reflex actions are automatic, protective responses mediated by a reflex arc through the spinal cord, bypassing conscious brain processing for speed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which endocrine gland releases thyroxine, a hormone that regulates the body's basal metabolic rate?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine, which controls the rate of cellular metabolism and influences growth and energy use throughout the body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The skeletal system performs all of the following functions EXCEPT
options: production of blood cells in the bone marrow
support and shape of the body
questions.explanation: Digestive enzymes are produced by glands such as the pancreas and intestinal walls, not by the skeletal system, whose functions are support, protection, movement, and haematopoiesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Homeostasis refers to the
options: conversion of light energy into chemical energy
maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes
process of cell division for growth
movement of an organism towards a stimulus
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions such as temperature, pH, and water balance to keep them relatively constant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which mechanism helps the human body lose excess heat when the environmental temperature rises?
options: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and increased sweating
Erection of hair by arrector pili muscles
questions.explanation: Vasodilation brings more blood close to the skin surface for heat loss, while evaporating sweat further cools the body, both countering overheating.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The muscular, ring-like sphincter that regulates the passage of food from the stomach into the duodenum is the
questions.explanation: The pyloric sphincter controls the release of partially digested food (chyme) from the stomach into the duodenum in regulated amounts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In flowering plants, the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a different flower on a different plant is termed
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination specifically involves pollen moving between flowers on genetically different plants, promoting genetic variation, unlike self-pollination within the same plant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The male gamete in flowering plants is produced within the
questions.explanation: Pollen grains contain the generative cell that divides to produce the male gametes (sperm nuclei) used in fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants, results in the formation of
options: a diploid zygote and a triploid endosperm
questions.explanation: One male nucleus fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, while the second fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm, nourishing the embryo.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following floral features is typically associated with wind-pollinated flowers?
options: Enclosed anthers hidden deep within the flower
Large, brightly coloured petals with scent and nectar
Sticky pollen produced in small quantities
Small, dull petals with feathery stigmas and large amounts of light pollen
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers rely on air currents, so they produce copious light, dry pollen and have exposed feathery stigmas rather than showy attractants for insects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In the human male reproductive system, sperm cells are produced within the
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis, the production of sperm cells, occurs in the seminiferous tubules located within the testes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the
questions.explanation: The sperm typically meets and fertilises the egg in the upper region of the fallopian tube shortly after ovulation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The hormone primarily responsible for maintaining the uterine lining during early pregnancy is
questions.explanation: Progesterone, secreted first by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, maintains the thickened, vascularised endometrium needed to sustain pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which structure in the human female reproductive system provides the site of exchange of nutrients and waste between mother and fetus?
questions.explanation: The placenta is a specialised organ allowing diffusion of nutrients, gases, and waste products between maternal and fetal blood without the two mixing directly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Vegetative propagation, such as the use of stem cuttings in cassava, is an example of
questions.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces new plants from vegetative parts of a single parent without fusion of gametes, making it a form of asexual reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A major disadvantage of asexual reproduction compared with sexual reproduction is that it
options: produces offspring genetically identical to the parent, reducing variation
questions.explanation: Because asexual reproduction lacks gamete fusion, offspring are clones of the parent, limiting genetic variation and adaptability to changing conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, the process by which a mature ovum is released from the Graafian follicle is called
questions.explanation: Ovulation is the release of a secondary oocyte from the ruptured Graafian follicle, typically around the midpoint of the menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes metamorphosis in insects such as the housefly?
options: Asexual budding from an adult insect
A single moult that converts a larva directly into an adult
A series of developmental stage changes from egg through larva and pupa to adult
Direct development with no larval stage
questions.explanation: Complete metamorphosis, as in the housefly, passes through egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages, each morphologically distinct from the others.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The function of the amniotic fluid surrounding a developing human fetus is mainly to
options: cushion and protect the fetus from mechanical shock
supply oxygen directly to fetal blood
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid acts as a shock absorber, protecting the developing fetus from physical impact and allowing free movement within the uterus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of these is an example of internal fertilisation?
options: Fertilisation in mammals, where sperm are deposited inside the female's body
Fertilisation in frogs during amplexus in water
Fertilisation in sea urchins releasing gametes into the ocean
Fertilisation in most bony fish, where gametes are released into water
questions.explanation: Internal fertilisation occurs within the female's reproductive tract, as in mammals, reducing gamete wastage compared with external fertilisation in water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Seed dormancy in flowering plants primarily allows a seed to
options: delay germination until environmental conditions become favourable
produce vegetative offshoots instead of seeds
questions.explanation: Dormancy is a survival mechanism that keeps a seed metabolically inactive until temperature, moisture, and light conditions favour successful germination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: According to Mendel's law of segregation, the two alleles for a trait
options: must always be identical in a diploid organism
separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele
are inherited only from the mother
always blend to form an intermediate phenotype
questions.explanation: Mendel's law of segregation states that allele pairs separate during meiosis, so each gamete receives only one allele for each gene.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous (Tt) tall pea plants, what proportion of the offspring is expected to be homozygous recessive?
questions.explanation: A Tt x Tt cross yields a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (TT:Tt:tt), so 1/4 of the offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive (tt).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between a homozygous dominant individual and a homozygous recessive individual for a single trait is called a
questions.explanation: A monohybrid cross examines the inheritance of a single gene/trait between two parents, as in Mendel's classic pea experiments.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A test cross is performed mainly to determine
options: whether an individual showing the dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous
the exact chromosome number of a species
the rate of mutation in a population
questions.explanation: Crossing an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual reveals, from the offspring ratio, whether the tested parent is homozygous or heterozygous dominant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best defines a phenotype?
options: The complete set of genes an organism carries
The exact location of a gene on a chromosome
The process by which alleles segregate during meiosis
The observable physical or biochemical characteristics of an organism
questions.explanation: Phenotype refers to the outward, observable expression of an organism's genotype interacting with its environment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Sickle cell anaemia in humans is inherited as an example of
questions.explanation: Heterozygotes (HbAHbS) express both normal and sickle haemoglobin, showing a form of codominance/incomplete dominance rather than simple dominant-recessive inheritance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele located on the
questions.explanation: Colour blindness is a classic X-linked recessive trait, which is why it occurs far more frequently in males, who have only one X chromosome.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between a heterozygous round, yellow pea plant (RrYy) and another heterozygous round, yellow plant, considering two independently assorting traits, is an example of a
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross tracks the simultaneous inheritance of two different traits, as Mendel did with seed shape and colour in peas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Mutation is best defined as
options: the blending of parental traits in offspring
the movement of chromosomes during mitosis only
the normal process of allele segregation during meiosis
a sudden, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA
questions.explanation: A mutation is any random, heritable alteration in the DNA sequence, which can arise spontaneously or be induced by mutagens, and is a source of new genetic variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a chromosomal mutation rather than a gene mutation?
options: Down syndrome, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21
Cystic fibrosis, caused by a deletion within a single gene
Sickle cell anaemia, caused by a single base substitution
Albinism, caused by a defective gene for melanin production
questions.explanation: Down syndrome results from trisomy 21, an abnormality in chromosome number, which is a chromosomal mutation, unlike single-gene mutations such as sickle cell anaemia.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a dihybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (RrYy x RrYy), the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring, assuming independent assortment, is
questions.explanation: Independent assortment of two gene pairs in a dihybrid cross produces the classic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which term describes different forms of the same gene occupying corresponding positions on homologous chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Alleles are alternative versions of a gene (for example, alleles for tall and short stature) found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A father with blood group AB and a mother with blood group OO can never have a child with blood group
questions.explanation: Since the AB parent contributes either allele A or allele B (never allele O) and the OO parent always contributes allele O, a child cannot be OO, hence cannot be blood group O.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Continuous variation, such as human height, typically results from
options: a single gene with two clearly distinct alleles
the combined effect of many genes (polygenic inheritance) interacting with environment
questions.explanation: Traits like height and skin colour show continuous variation because they are controlled by many genes acting together, further modified by environmental factors.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Discontinuous variation, such as human ABO blood grouping, is characterised by
options: identical expression in every individual of a species
distinct, non-overlapping categories usually controlled by one or few genes
a smooth range of intermediate values
questions.explanation: Discontinuous traits fall into clear-cut, qualitatively distinct categories (such as blood groups A, B, AB, O) typically governed by one or a small number of genes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The sum total of all living and non-living components interacting within a given environment is called a
questions.explanation: An ecosystem comprises the biotic community together with the abiotic (non-living) environment and the interactions between them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Organisms that manufacture their own organic food from inorganic raw materials, usually through photosynthesis, are called
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, are autotrophs that convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds, forming the base of food chains.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a food chain, organisms that feed directly on producers are known as
questions.explanation: Primary consumers (herbivores) occupy the second trophic level, feeding directly on producers such as green plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The organisms responsible for breaking down dead organic matter and releasing nutrients back into the ecosystem are called
questions.explanation: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead organisms and waste, recycling nutrients like nitrogen and carbon back into the ecosystem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Approximately what percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next in a typical food chain?
questions.explanation: The ten percent rule approximates that only about ten percent of energy at one trophic level is available to the next, the rest being lost mainly as heat through respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which term describes all the members of a single species living and interbreeding in a particular area at a given time?
questions.explanation: A population consists of individuals of one species occupying the same geographic area and capable of interbreeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The role and position an organism occupies within its ecosystem, including its interactions with other organisms and use of resources, is called its
questions.explanation: An ecological niche describes an organism's functional role, including its feeding habits, habitat use, and interactions, distinct from mere physical location (habitat).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria found in the root nodules of leguminous plants convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use, mainly
questions.explanation: Symbiotic bacteria such as Rhizobium fix atmospheric N2 into ammonia, which is then converted into forms like nitrates that plants can absorb and use.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In the carbon cycle, the process that returns carbon dioxide from living organisms back into the atmosphere is
questions.explanation: Respiration in plants, animals, and microorganisms breaks down organic molecules and releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere as a byproduct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which pyramid in ecology always shows a regular, upright shape because energy is always lost between trophic levels?
options: None of the pyramids are always upright
questions.explanation: Because energy transfer is never 100% efficient and energy is always lost as heat, the pyramid of energy is always upright, unlike pyramids of numbers or biomass which can sometimes be inverted.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of interspecific competition?
options: Bees pollinating flowers while feeding on nectar
Two male lions of the same pride fighting over a mate
A parasite living within its host with no benefit to the host
Lions and hyenas competing for the same prey in a savanna
questions.explanation: Interspecific competition occurs between individuals of different species competing for the same limited resource, such as lions and hyenas both hunting similar prey.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A symbiotic relationship in which one organism benefits while the other is harmed is called
questions.explanation: In parasitism, the parasite derives benefit (nutrients, shelter) at the direct expense and harm of its host organism.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which human activity is a major direct cause of desertification in the Sahel region?
options: Overgrazing and deforestation reducing vegetation cover
questions.explanation: Overgrazing and clearing of vegetation strip protective plant cover from soil, accelerating erosion and the southward spread of desert-like conditions in the Sahel.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Eutrophication of a water body is most directly caused by
options: removal of algae from the water surface
a sudden decrease in water temperature
an increase in dissolved oxygen concentration
excessive input of nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates from fertiliser runoff
questions.explanation: Nutrient enrichment, often from agricultural runoff, triggers algal blooms; their subsequent decomposition depletes dissolved oxygen, harming aquatic life.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which term best describes the variety of species, genes, and ecosystems within a given region?
questions.explanation: Biodiversity encompasses the full range of variation at the genetic, species, and ecosystem levels within an area.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Bioaccumulation of a non-biodegradable pesticide such as DDT along a food chain results in the
options: complete breakdown of the pesticide by decomposers
highest concentration occurring in top carnivores
pesticide being evenly distributed at every trophic level
questions.explanation: Because DDT resists breakdown and accumulates in tissues, its concentration magnifies at each successive trophic level, becoming most concentrated in top predators (biomagnification).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution proposes that species change over time mainly through
options: natural selection acting on heritable variation
deliberate selection by the organisms themselves
questions.explanation: Darwin proposed that individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully, gradually shifting a population's characteristics.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following best illustrates the concept of natural selection?
options: A gardener grafting two different plant varieties together
A farmer deliberately breeding only the largest cattle for meat production
Peppered moths of a darker colour became more common in polluted industrial areas where they were better camouflaged
Identical twins developing from a single fertilised egg
questions.explanation: Industrial melanism in peppered moths is a classic natural selection example: darker moths were better camouflaged against soot-darkened bark, so predators removed more of the paler moths, shifting population colour over generations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Lamarck's theory of evolution, now largely rejected, proposed that
options: mutations are the ultimate source of genetic variation
species remain fixed and unchanging over time
natural selection acts on existing heritable variation
characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime could be inherited by offspring
questions.explanation: Lamarck's theory of inheritance of acquired characteristics (e.g., a giraffe's neck lengthening from stretching and this being passed to offspring) is not supported by modern genetics.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following provides direct fossil evidence supporting the theory of evolution?
options: A graded sequence of fossils showing gradual anatomical change over geological time in rock strata
The presence of vestigial organs in living organisms
Comparable stages of embryonic development in different vertebrates
Similarities in the amino acid sequences of related species
questions.explanation: Fossil evidence for evolution comes from strata showing progressive morphological changes in related organisms across successive geological time periods, unlike the other options which are other lines (not fossil) evidence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Vestigial organs, such as the human appendix, are considered evidence for evolution because they
options: are found only in newly evolved species
are remnants of structures that were functional in ancestral organisms
always increase in size across generations
questions.explanation: Vestigial structures are reduced, often non-functional remnants of organs that served a purpose in an ancestral form, indicating common descent with modification.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Homologous structures, such as the forelimbs of a human, whale, and bat, provide evidence for evolution because they
options: share a similar basic bone structure despite differing functions, indicating a common ancestor
perform identical functions across all species
arose completely independently with no shared ancestry
are found only in unrelated groups of organisms
questions.explanation: Homologous structures have the same underlying skeletal plan inherited from a common ancestor, even though they have been modified for different functions such as swimming, flying, or grasping.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Analogous structures, such as the wings of a bird and the wings of an insect, arise through
options: convergent evolution, where unrelated organisms evolve similar features independently
divergent evolution from a recent common ancestor
identical genetic mechanisms in both groups
questions.explanation: Analogous structures perform similar functions but evolved independently in unrelated lineages facing similar environmental pressures, a pattern called convergent evolution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered a mechanism that can drive evolutionary change within a population?
options: Identical reproductive success for every individual regardless of trait
Complete isolation preventing any gene flow or mutation
Perfectly stable environmental conditions with no selection pressure
Mutation introducing new alleles into the gene pool
questions.explanation: Mutation is the ultimate source of new genetic variation, upon which natural selection, genetic drift, and gene flow can act to drive evolutionary change.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Genetic drift is best described as
options: random fluctuations in allele frequencies, especially pronounced in small populations
the movement of individuals between populations
the process by which acquired traits become heritable
the directed change in allele frequency caused solely by natural selection
questions.explanation: Genetic drift refers to chance changes in allele frequency from generation to generation, with effects that are much stronger in small populations than in large ones.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Reproductive isolation between two populations of the same ancestral species, leading eventually to the formation of new species, is called
options: adaptive radiation restricted to one species
questions.explanation: Speciation is the evolutionary process by which populations evolve to become distinct species, often following prolonged reproductive isolation such as geographic separation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Adaptive radiation, as classically illustrated by Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands, refers to
options: the extinction of a species due to competition
the transfer of genes between two different species
the convergence of unrelated species toward one form
the diversification of a single ancestral species into many species occupying different ecological niches
questions.explanation: Adaptive radiation occurs when one ancestral lineage rapidly diversifies into multiple species, each adapted to exploit a different ecological niche, as seen in the varied beak shapes of Darwin's finches.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Comparative embryology provides evidence for evolution mainly because
options: all embryos of different species are visibly identical at every developmental stage
embryonic development has no connection to evolutionary ancestry
related organisms often show striking similarities in their early embryonic stages
embryos of unrelated species never show any structural similarity
questions.explanation: Vertebrate embryos, including humans and fish, show similar early features such as gill slits and tails, reflecting shared evolutionary ancestry despite differing adult forms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes a population in which allele frequencies remain constant from generation to generation, provided that
options: there is no mutation, migration, selection, or genetic drift, and mating is random
individuals mate only with close relatives
natural selection is actively favouring one allele
the population size is very small
questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a theoretical baseline assuming no evolutionary forces (mutation, migration, selection, drift) and random mating; deviations from it indicate evolution is occurring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Biochemical evidence, such as comparing cytochrome-c protein sequences across species, supports evolution by showing that
options: only fossil evidence can indicate evolutionary relationships
all species have identical protein sequences regardless of relatedness
species with more similar sequences are generally more closely related evolutionarily
protein sequences provide no useful information about ancestry
questions.explanation: The degree of similarity in conserved proteins like cytochrome-c correlates with evolutionary relatedness; closely related species tend to show fewer amino acid differences.
